In 2009, a paper was published suggesting a new definition for the word 'volcano' that includes processes such as [cryovolcanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryovolcanism). It suggested that a volcano be defined as 'an opening on a planet or moon's surface from which [magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma), as defined for that body, and/or magmatic gas is erupted.'

## Etymology and terminology

The word *volcano* ([UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English): [/vɒlˈkeɪnəʊ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English); [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English): [/vɑːlˈkeɪnoʊ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English)) originates from the early 17th century, derived from the Italian name *[Vulcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcano)*, a [volcanic island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_island) in the [Aeolian Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeolian_Islands) of Italy, which in turn comes from the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin) name *[Volcānus](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Volcanus#Latin)* or *[Vulcānus](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Vulcanus#Latin)*, referring to [Vulcan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcan_%28mythology%29), the god of fire in [Roman mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_mythology).

The set of processes and phenomena involved in volcanic activity is called [volcanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism) \[early 19th century: from *volcano* + *-ism*\]. The study of volcanism and volcanoes is called [volcanology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanology) \[mid-19th century: from *volcano* + *-logy*\], sometimes spelled *vulcanology*.

## Plate tectonics

According to the theory of plate tectonics, Earth's [lithosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithosphere), its rigid outer shell, is broken into sixteen larger and several smaller plates. These move continuously at a slow pace, due to [convection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convection) in the underlying ductile [mantle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_mantle), and most volcanic activity on Earth takes place along plate boundaries, where plates are converging (and lithosphere is being destroyed) or are diverging (and new lithosphere is being created).

During the development of geological theory, certain concepts that allowed the grouping of volcanoes in time, place, structure and composition have developed that ultimately have had to be explained in the theory of plate tectonics. For example, some volcanoes are *[polygenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygenetic_volcanic_field)* with more than one period of activity during their history; other volcanoes that become extinct after erupting exactly once are *[monogenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogenetic_volcanic_field)* (meaning "one life") and such volcanoes are often grouped together in a geographical region.

### Divergent plate boundaries

At the [mid-ocean ridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-ocean_ridge), two [tectonic plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tectonic_plates) diverge from one another as hot mantle rock creeps upwards beneath the thinned [oceanic crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_crust). The decrease of pressure in the rising mantle rock leads to [adiabatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adiabatic) expansion and the [partial melting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_melting) of the rock, causing volcanism and creating new oceanic crust. Most [divergent plate boundaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_plate_boundaries) are at the bottom of the oceans, and so most volcanic activity on Earth is submarine, forming new [seafloor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafloor). [Black smokers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_smoker) (also known as deep sea vents) are evidence of this kind of volcanic activity. Where the mid-oceanic ridge is above sea level, volcanic islands are formed, such as [Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland).

### Convergent plate boundaries

[Subduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subduction) zones are places where two plates, usually an oceanic plate and a continental plate, collide. The oceanic plate subducts (dives beneath the continental plate), forming a deep ocean trench just offshore. In a process called [flux melting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flux_melting), water released from the subducting plate lowers the melting temperature of the overlying mantle wedge, thus creating [magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma). This magma tends to be extremely [viscous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscous) because of its high [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica) content, so it often does not reach the surface but [cools and solidifies at depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous_intrusion). When it does reach the surface, however, a volcano is formed. Thus subduction zones are bordered by chains of volcanoes called [volcanic arcs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_arc). Typical examples are the volcanoes in the Pacific [Ring of Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire), such as the [Cascade Volcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascade_Volcanoes) or the [Japanese archipelago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_archipelago), or the eastern islands of [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia).

### Hotspots

[Hotspots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotspot_%28geology%29) are volcanic areas thought to be formed by [mantle plumes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantle_plume), which are hypothesized to be columns of hot material rising from the core-mantle boundary. As with mid-ocean ridges, the rising mantle rock experiences decompression melting which generates large volumes of magma. Because tectonic plates move across mantle plumes, each volcano becomes inactive as it drifts off the plume, and new volcanoes are created where the plate advances over the plume. The [Hawaiian Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Islands) are thought to have been formed in such a manner, as has the [Snake River Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake_River_Plain), with the [Yellowstone Caldera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera) being part of the North American plate currently above the [Yellowstone hotspot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_hotspot). However, the mantle plume hypothesis has been questioned.

### Continental rifting

Sustained upwelling of hot mantle rock can develop under the interior of a continent and lead to rifting. Early stages of rifting are characterized by [flood basalts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_basalt) and may progress to the point where a tectonic plate is completely split. A divergent plate boundary then develops between the two-halves of the split plate. However, rifting often fails to completely split the continental lithosphere (such as in an [aulacogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aulacogen)), and failed rifts are characterized by volcanoes that erupt unusual [alkali lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_magma_series) or [carbonatites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbonatite). Examples include the volcanoes of the [East African Rift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Rift).

## Volcanic features

A volcano needs a reservoir of molten magma (e.g. a [magma chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma_chamber)), a conduit to allow magma to rise through the crust, and a vent to allow the magma to escape above the surface as lava. The erupted volcanic material (lava and tephra) that is deposited around the vent is known as a **volcanic edifice**, typically a volcanic cone or mountain.

The most common perception of a volcano is of a [conical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conical) mountain, spewing [lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava) and poisonous [gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_gas) from a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_crater) at its summit; however, this describes just one of the many types of volcano. The features of volcanoes are varied. The structure and behaviour of volcanoes depend on several factors. Some volcanoes have rugged peaks formed by [lava domes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava_dome) rather than a summit crater while others have [landscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landscape) features such as massive [plateaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau). Vents that issue volcanic material (including lava and [ash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_ash)) and gases (mainly steam and magmatic gases) can develop anywhere on the [landform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landform) and may give rise to smaller cones such as [Puʻu ʻŌʻō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puʻu_ʻŌʻō) on a flank of [Kīlauea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kīlauea) in Hawaii. [Volcanic craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_crater) are not always at the top of a mountain or hill and may be filled with lakes such as with [Lake Taupō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Taupō) in New Zealand. Some volcanoes can be low-relief landform features, with the potential to be hard to recognize as such and be obscured by geological processes.

Other types of volcano include [mud volcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud_volcano), which are structures often not associated with known magmatic activity; and [cryovolcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryovolcano) (or ice volcanoes), particularly on some moons of [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter), [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn), and [Neptune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune). Active mud volcanoes tend to involve temperatures much lower than those of [igneous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous) volcanoes except when the mud volcano is actually a vent of an igneous volcano.

### Fissure vents

[Volcanic fissure vents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fissure_vent) are generally found at [diverging plate boundaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_boundary), they are flat, linear fractures through which [basaltic lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basaltic_lava) emerges. These kinds of volcanoes are non-explosive and the basaltic lava tends to have a low viscosity and solidifies slowly leading to a gentle sloping basaltic [lava plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_plateau). They often relate or constitute shield volcanoes

### Shield volcanoes

Shield volcanoes, so named for their broad, shield-like profiles, are formed by the eruption of low-viscosity basaltic or andesitic lava that can flow a great distance from a vent. They generally do not explode catastrophically but are characterized by relatively gentle [effusive eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effusive_eruption). Since low-viscosity magma is typically low in silica, shield volcanoes are more common in oceanic than continental settings. The Hawaiian volcanic chain is a series of shield cones, and they are common in [Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland), as well. [Olympus Mons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympus_Mons), an extinct martian shield volcano is the largest known volcano in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System).

### Lava domes

[Lava domes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava_dome), also called dome volcanoes, have steep convex sides built by slow eruptions of highly viscous lava, for example, [rhyolite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyolite). They are sometimes formed within the crater of a previous volcanic eruption, as in the case of [Mount St. Helens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_St._Helens), but can also form independently, as in the case of [Lassen Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lassen_Peak). Like stratovolcanoes, they can produce violent, explosive eruptions, but the lava generally does not flow far from the originating vent.

### Cryptodomes

Cryptodomes are formed when viscous lava is forced upward causing the surface to bulge. The [1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens) was an example; lava beneath the surface of the mountain created an upward bulge, which later collapsed down the north side of the mountain.

### Cinder cones

Cinder cones result from eruptions of mostly small pieces of [scoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoria) and [pyroclastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroclastic_rock) (both resemble cinders, hence the name of this volcano type) that build up around the vent. These can be relatively short-lived eruptions that produce a cone-shaped hill perhaps 30 to 400 metres (100 to 1,300 ft) high. Most cinder cones erupt only once and some may be found in [monogenetic volcanic fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogenetic_volcanic_field) that may include other features that form when magma comes into contact with water such as [maar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maar) explosion craters and [tuff rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuff_ring). Cinder cones may form as [flank vents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasitic_cone) on larger volcanoes, or occur on their own. [Parícutin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parícutin) in Mexico and [Sunset Crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset_Crater) in [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona) are examples of cinder cones. In [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico), [Caja del Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caja_del_Rio) is a [volcanic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_field) of over 60 cinder cones.

Based on satellite images, it has been suggested that cinder cones might occur on other terrestrial bodies in the Solar system too; on the surface of Mars and the Moon.

### Stratovolcanoes (composite volcanoes)

Stratovolcanoes are tall conical mountains composed of lava flows and [tephra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tephra) in alternate layers, the [strata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strata) that gives rise to the name. They are also known as *composite volcanoes* because they are created from multiple structures during different kinds of eruptions; the main conduit bringing magma to the surface branches into multiple secondary conduits and occasional [laccoliths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laccolith) or [sills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sill_%28geology%29), the branching conduits may form [parasitic cones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasitic_cone) on the flanks of the main cone. Classic examples include [Mount Fuji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji) in Japan, [Mayon Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayon_Volcano) in the Philippines, and [Mount Vesuvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Vesuvius) and [Stromboli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stromboli) in Italy.

[Ash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_ash) produced by the [explosive eruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosive_eruption) of stratovolcanoes has [historically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recorded_history) posed the greatest volcanic hazard to civilizations. The lavas of stratovolcanoes are higher in silica, and therefore much more viscous, than lavas from shield volcanoes. High-silica lavas also tend to contain more dissolved gas. The combination is deadly, promoting explosive eruptions that produce great quantities of ash, as well as [pyroclastic surges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroclastic_surge) like the one that destroyed the city of Saint-Pierre in Martinique in 1902. They are also steeper than shield volcanoes, with slopes of 30–35° compared to slopes of generally 5–10°, and their loose [tephra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tephra) are material for dangerous [lahars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahar). Large pieces of tephra are called [volcanic bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_bomb). Big bombs can measure more than 1.2 metres (4 ft) across and weigh several tons.

### Supervolcanoes

A supervolcano is defined as a volcano that has experienced one or more eruptions that produced over 1,000 cubic kilometres (240 cu mi) of volcanic deposits in a single explosive event. Such eruptions occur when a very large magma chamber full of gas-rich, silicic magma is emptied in a catastrophic [caldera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldera)-forming eruption. Ash flow [tuffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuff) emplaced by such eruptions are the only volcanic product with volumes rivalling those of [flood basalts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_basalt).

Supervolcano eruptions, while the most dangerous type, are very rare; [four are known from the last million years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervolcano#Known_super_eruptions), and about 60 historical VEI 8 eruptions have been identified in the geologic record over millions of years. A supervolcano can produce devastation on a continental scale, and severely cool global temperatures for many years after the eruption due to the huge volumes of [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur) and ash released into the atmosphere.

Because of the enormous area they cover, and subsequent concealment under vegetation and glacial deposits, supervolcanoes can be difficult to identify in the geologic record without careful [geological mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geological_map). Known examples include [Yellowstone Caldera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera) in [Yellowstone National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_National_Park) and [Valles Caldera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valles_Caldera) in [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico) (both western United States); [Lake Taupō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Taupō) in New Zealand; [Lake Toba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Toba) in [Sumatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatra), Indonesia; and [Ngorongoro Crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngorongoro_Crater) in Tanzania.

#### Caldera volcanoes

Volcanoes that, though large, are not large enough to be called supervolcanoes, may also form calderas (collapsed crater) in the same way. There may be active or dormant cones inside of the caldera or even a lake, such lakes are called [Volcanogenic lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanogenic_lake), or simply, volcanic lakes.

### Submarine volcanoes

Submarine volcanoes are common features of the ocean floor. Volcanic activity during the [Holocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocene) Epoch has been documented at only 119 submarine volcanoes, but there may be more than one million geologically young submarine volcanoes on the ocean floor. In shallow water, active volcanoes disclose their presence by blasting steam and rocky debris high above the ocean's surface. In the deep ocean basins, the tremendous weight of the water prevents the explosive release of steam and gases; however, submarine eruptions can be detected by [hydrophones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrophone) and by the discoloration of water because of [volcanic gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_gas). [Pillow lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillow_lava) is a common eruptive product of submarine volcanoes and is characterized by thick sequences of discontinuous pillow-shaped masses which form underwater. Even large submarine eruptions may not disturb the ocean surface, due to the rapid cooling effect and increased buoyancy in water (as compared to air), which often causes volcanic vents to form steep pillars on the ocean floor. [Hydrothermal vents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal_vent) are common near these volcanoes, and [some support peculiar ecosystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_smoker) based on [chemotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemotroph) feeding on dissolved minerals. Over time, the formations created by submarine volcanoes may become so large that they break the ocean surface as new islands or floating [pumice rafts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pumice_raft).

In May and June 2018, a multitude of [seismic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seismic) signals were detected by earthquake monitoring agencies all over the world. They took the form of unusual humming sounds, and some of the signals detected in November of that year had a duration of up to 20 minutes. An [oceanographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanographic) research campaign in May 2019 showed that the previously mysterious humming noises were caused by the formation of a submarine volcano off the coast of [Mayotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayotte).

### Subglacial volcanoes

Subglacial volcanoes develop underneath [ice caps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_cap). They are made up of lava plateaus capping extensive pillow lavas and [palagonite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palagonite). These volcanoes are also called table mountains, [tuyas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuya), or (in Iceland) mobergs. Very good examples of this type of volcano can be seen in Iceland and in [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia). The origin of the term comes from [Tuya Butte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuya_Butte), which is one of the several tuyas in the area of the [Tuya River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuya_River) and [Tuya Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuya_Range) in northern British Columbia. Tuya Butte was the first such [landform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landform) analysed and so its name has entered the geological literature for this kind of volcanic formation. The [Tuya Mountains Provincial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuya_Mountains_Provincial_Park) was recently established to protect this unusual landscape, which lies north of [Tuya Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuya_Lake) and south of the [Jennings River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennings_River) near the boundary with the [Yukon Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukon_Territory).

### Hydrothermal features

Hydrothermal features, for example [geysers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geyser), [fumaroles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumarole), [mud pools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudpot), [mud volcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud_volcano), [hot springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_spring) and acidic hot springs involve water as well as geothermal or magmatic activity. Such features are common around volcanoes and are often indicative of volcanism.

#### Mud volcanoes

[Mud volcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud_volcano) or mud domes are conical structures created by eruption of liquids and gases, particularly mud (slurries), water and gases, although several activities may contribute. The largest mud volcanoes are 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) in diameter and reach 700 metres (2,300 ft) high. Mud volcanoes can be seen off the shore of [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia), on the island of [Baratang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baratang_Island), in [Balochistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balochistan,_Pakistan) and in central Asia.

#### Fumarole

[Fumaroles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumarole) are vents on the surface from which hot steam and volcanic gases erupt due to the presence of superheated groundwater, these may indicate volcanic activity. Fumaroles erupting sulfurous gases are also often called solfataras.

#### Geysers

Geysers are springs which will occasionally erupt and discharge hot water and steam. Geysers may indicate ongoing magmatism, water underground is heated by hot rocks and [steam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam) [pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapor_pressure) builds up before being released along with a jet of hot water. Almost half of all active geysers are present in Yellowstone National Park, US.

## Erupted material

The material that is expelled in a [volcanic eruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_eruption) can be classified into three types:

1. [Volcanic gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_gas), a mixture made mostly of [steam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam), [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide), and a sulfur compound (either [sulfur dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur_dioxide), SO2, or [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide), H2S, depending on the temperature)
2. [Lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava), the name of magma when it emerges and flows over the surface
3. [Tephra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tephra), particles of solid material of all shapes and sizes ejected and thrown through the air

### Volcanic gases

The concentrations of different [volcanic gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_gas) can vary considerably from one volcano to the next. [Water vapour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_vapour) is typically the most abundant volcanic gas, followed by [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide) and [sulfur dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur_dioxide). Other principal volcanic gases include [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide), [hydrogen chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_chloride), and [hydrogen fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_fluoride). A large number of minor and trace gases are also found in volcanic emissions, for example [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen), [carbon monoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_monoxide), [halocarbons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halocarbon), organic compounds, and [volatile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatile_%28astrogeology%29) metal chlorides.

### Lava flows

The form and style of an eruption of a volcano is largely determined by the composition of the lava it erupts. The viscosity (how fluid the lava is) and the amount of dissolved gas are the most important characteristics of magma, and both are largely determined by the amount of silica in the magma. Magma rich in silica is much more viscous than silica-poor magma, and silica-rich magma also tends to contain more dissolved gases.

Lava can be broadly classified into four different compositions:

- If the erupted [magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma) contains a high percentage (\>63%) of [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica), the lava is described as *[felsic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felsic)*. Felsic lavas ([dacites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacite) or [rhyolites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyolite)) are highly [viscous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscous) and are erupted as domes or short, stubby flows. [Lassen Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lassen_Peak) in California is an example of a volcano formed from felsic lava and is actually a large lava dome.

- If the erupted magma contains 52–63% silica, the lava is of *[intermediate composition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate_composition)* or *[andesitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andesitic)*. Intermediate magmas are characteristic of stratovolcanoes. They are most commonly formed at [convergent boundaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_boundaries) between [tectonic plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tectonic_plate), by several processes. One process is the hydration melting of mantle peridotite followed by fractional crystallization. Water from a subducting [slab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slab_%28geology%29) rises into the overlying mantle, lowering its melting point, particularly for the more silica-rich minerals. Fractional crystallization further enriches the magma in silica. It has also been suggested that intermediate magmas are produced by the melting of sediments carried downward by the subducted slab. Another process is magma mixing between felsic rhyolitic and mafic basaltic magmas in an intermediate reservoir before emplacement or lava flow.
- If the erupted magma contains \<52% and \>45% silica, the lava is called *[mafic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafic)* (because it contains higher percentages of [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium) (Mg) and iron (Fe)) or [basaltic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt). These lavas are usually hotter and much less viscous than felsic lavas. Mafic magmas are formed by partial melting of the dry mantle, with limited fractional crystallization and assimilation of crustal material.

- Some erupted magmas contain ≤45% silica and produce *[ultramafic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultramafic)* lava. Ultramafic flows, also known as [komatiites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komatiite), are very rare; indeed, very few have been erupted at Earth's surface since the [Proterozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proterozoic), when the planet's heat flow was higher. They are (or were) the hottest lavas, and were probably more fluid than common mafic lavas, with a viscosity less than a tenth that of hot basalt magma.

Mafic lava flows show two varieties of surface texture: ʻAʻa (pronounced [\[ˈʔaʔa\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Hawaiian)) and [pāhoehoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pāhoehoe) ([\[paːˈho.eˈho.e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Hawaiian)), both [Hawaiian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_language) words. ʻAʻa is characterized by a rough, clinkery surface and is the typical texture of cooler basalt lava flows. Pāhoehoe is characterized by its smooth and often ropey or wrinkly surface and is generally formed from more fluid lava flows. Pāhoehoe flows are sometimes observed to transition to ʻaʻa flows as they move away from the vent, but never the reverse.

More silicic lava flows take the form of block lava, where the flow is covered with angular, vesicle-poor blocks. [Rhyolitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyolitic) flows typically consist largely of [obsidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obsidian).

### Tephra

Tephra is made when magma inside the volcano is blown apart by the rapid expansion of hot volcanic gases. Magma commonly explodes as the gas dissolved in it comes out of solution as the pressure decreases [when it flows to the surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrusion). These violent explosions produce particles of material that can then fly from the volcano. Solid particles smaller than 2 mm in diameter ([sand-sized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand) or smaller) are called volcanic ash.

Tephra and other [volcaniclastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcaniclastics) (shattered volcanic material) make up more of the volume of many volcanoes than do lava flows. Volcaniclastics may have contributed as much as a third of all sedimentation in the geologic record. The production of large volumes of tephra is characteristic of explosive volcanism.

### Dissection

Through natural processes, mainly [erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erosion), so much of the solidified erupted material that makes up the mantle of a volcano may be stripped away that its inner anatomy becomes apparent. Using the metaphor of [biological anatomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatomy), such a process is called "dissection". When the volcano is extinct, a plug forms on its vent, over time due to erosion, the volcanic cone slowly erodes away leaving the resistant lava plug intact. [Cinder Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinder_Hill), a feature of [Mount Bird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Bird) on [Ross Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Island), [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica), is a prominent example of a dissected volcano. Volcanoes that were, on a geological timescale, recently active, such as for example [Mount Kaimon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kaimon) in southern [Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyūshū), Japan, tend to be undissected. [Devils Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devils_Tower) in Wyoming is a famous example of exposed volcanic plug.

## Volcanic eruptions

As of August 2026, the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution)'s [Global Volcanism Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Volcanism_Program) database of volcanic eruptions in the [Holocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocene) [Epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoch_%28geology%29) (the last 11,700 years) lists 10,652 confirmed eruptions from 1,214 volcanoes. The database also lists 1,113 uncertain eruptions and 168 discredited eruptions for the same time interval.

Eruption styles are broadly divided into magmatic, phreatomagmatic (hydrovolcanic), and phreatic eruptions. The intensity of explosive volcanism is expressed using the [volcanic explosivity index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_explosivity_index) (VEI), which ranges from 0 for Hawaiian-type eruptions to 8 for supervolcanic eruptions:

- Magmatic eruptions are driven primarily by gas release due to decompression. Low-viscosity magma with little dissolved gas produces relatively gentle effusive eruptions. High-viscosity magma with a high content of dissolved gas produces violent [explosive eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosive_eruption). The range of observed eruption styles is expressed from historical examples.
- [Hawaiian eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_eruption) are typical of volcanoes that erupt mafic lava with a relatively low gas content. These are almost entirely effusive, producing local [lava fountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava_fountain) and highly fluid lava flows but relatively little tephra. They are named after the [Hawaiian volcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_hotspot). The eruption column from these eruptions does not exceed 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) in height.
- [Strombolian eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strombolian_eruption) are characterized by moderate viscosities and dissolved gas levels. They are characterized by frequent but short-lived eruptions that can produce eruptive columns hundreds of meters high, which can also be seen in a [gas slug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_slug). Their primary product is [scoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoria). They are named after [Stromboli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stromboli).
- [Vulcanian eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcanian_eruption) are characterized by yet higher viscosities and partial crystallization of magma, which is often intermediate in composition. Eruptions take the form of short-lived explosions for several hours, which destroy a central dome and eject large lava blocks and bombs. This is followed by an effusive phase that rebuilds the central dome. Vulcanian eruptions are named after [Vulcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcano). Eruption columns from these eruptions do not exceed 20 kilometres (12 mi) in height.
- [Peléan eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peléan_eruption) are more violent still, being characterized by dome growth and collapse that produces various kinds of pyroclastic flows. They are named after [Mount Pelée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pelée).
- [Plinian eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plinian_eruption) are characterized by sustained huge eruption columns whose collapse produces catastrophic pyroclastic flows. They are named after [Pliny the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Younger), who chronicled the Plinian [eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eruption_of_Mount_Vesuvius_in_79) AD.
- Ultra-Plinian eruptions are the largest of all volcanic eruptions are more intense, have a higher eruption rate than Plinian ones, form higher eruption columns and may form large calderas. These eruptions produce rhyolitic lava, tephra, [pumice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pumice) and thick pyroclastic flows that cover vast areas and may produce widespread [ash-fall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_ash) deposits. Examples are [Mt. Mazama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Mazama) and Yellowstone.
- [Phreatomagmatic eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phreatomagmatic_eruption) (hydrovolcanic) are characterized by interaction of rising magma with [groundwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater). They are driven by the resulting rapid buildup of pressure in the [superheated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superheating) groundwater.
- [Phreatic eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phreatic_eruption) are characterized by superheating of groundwater that comes in contact with hot rock or magma. They are distinguished from phreatomagmatic eruptions because the erupted material is all [country rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_rock_%28geology%29); no magma is erupted.

## Volcanic activity

Volcanoes vary greatly in their level of activity, with individual volcanic systems having an *eruption recurrence* ranging from several times a year to once in tens of thousands of years. Volcanoes are informally described as **erupting**, **active**, **dormant**, or **extinct**, but the definitions of these terms are not entirely uniform among volcanologists. The level of activity of most volcanoes falls upon a graduated spectrum, with much overlap between categories, and does not always fit neatly into only one of these three separate categories.

### Erupting

The [USGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USGS) defines a volcano as "erupting" whenever the ejection of magma from any point on the volcano is visible, including visible magma still contained within the walls of the summit crater.

### Active

While there is no international consensus among volcanologists on how to define an active volcano, the USGS defines a volcano as *active* whenever subterranean indicators, such as [earthquake swarms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake_swarm), ground inflation, or unusually high levels of carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide are present.

### Dormant and reactivated

The USGS defines a dormant volcano as any volcano that is not showing any signs of unrest such as earthquake swarms, ground swelling, or excessive noxious gas emissions, but which shows signs that it could yet become active again. Many dormant volcanoes have not erupted for thousands of years, but have still shown signs that they may be likely to erupt again in the future. Technically, any volcano that is dormant is also considered to be geologically "active".

In an article justifying the re-classification of Alaska's [Mount Edgecumbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Edgecumbe_%28Alaska%29) volcano from "dormant" to "active", volcanologists at the [Alaska Volcano Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Volcano_Observatory) pointed out that the term "dormant" in reference to volcanoes has been deprecated over the past few decades and that "\[t\]he term "dormant volcano" is so little used and undefined in modern volcanology that the Encyclopedia of Volcanoes (2000) does not contain it in the glossaries or index", however the USGS still widely employs the term.

Previously a volcano was often considered to be extinct if there were no written records of its activity. Such a generalization is inconsistent with observation and deeper study, as has occurred recently with the unexpected eruption of the [Chaitén volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaitén_%28volcano%29) in 2008. Modern volcanic activity monitoring techniques, and improvements in the modelling of the factors that produce eruptions, have helped the understanding of why volcanoes may remain dormant for a long time, and then become unexpectedly active again. The potential for eruptions, and their style, depend mainly upon the state of the magma storage system under the volcano, the eruption trigger mechanism and its timescale. For example, the [Yellowstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera) volcano has a repose/recharge period of around 700,000 years, and [Toba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toba_Lake) of around 380,000 years. [Vesuvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesuvius) was described by Roman writers as having been covered with gardens and vineyards before its unexpected [eruption of 79 CE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eruption_of_Mount_Vesuvius_in_79), which destroyed the towns of [Herculaneum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculaneum) and [Pompeii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeii).

Accordingly, it can sometimes be difficult to distinguish between an extinct volcano and a dormant (inactive) one. Long volcano dormancy is known to decrease awareness. [Pinatubo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinatubo) was an inconspicuous volcano, unknown to most people in the surrounding areas, and initially not seismically monitored before its unanticipated and catastrophic eruption of 1991. Two other examples of volcanoes that were once thought to be extinct, before springing back into eruptive activity were the long-dormant [Soufrière Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soufrière_Hills) volcano on the island of [Montserrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montserrat), thought to be extinct until activity resumed in 1995 (turning its capital [Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth,_Montserrat) into a [ghost town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_town)) and [Fourpeaked Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourpeaked_Mountain) in Alaska, which, before its September 2006 eruption, had not erupted since before 8000 BCE. Another example is the [Taftan volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taftan_%28volcano%29) in southwestern Iran. This volcano was long thought by volcanologists to be extinct, with its last eruption having occurred an estimated 710,000 years ago. However, beginning around June 2023, the volcano began experiencing uplifting near its summit, suggesting that the volcano was dormant.

### Extinct

Extinct volcanoes are those that scientists consider unlikely to erupt again because the volcano no longer has a magma supply. Examples of extinct volcanoes are many volcanoes on the [Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian–Emperor_seamount_chain) in the Pacific Ocean (although some volcanoes at the eastern end of the chain are active), [Hohentwiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hohentwiel) in Germany, [Shiprock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiprock) in [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico), U.S., [Capulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capulin_Volcano_National_Monument) in New Mexico, U.S., [Zuidwal volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuidwal_volcano) in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands), and many volcanoes in Italy such as [Monte Vulture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Vulture). [Edinburgh Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Castle) in Scotland is located atop an extinct volcano, which forms [Castle Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Rock_%28Edinburgh%29). Whether a volcano is truly extinct is often difficult to determine. Since "supervolcano" [calderas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldera) can have eruptive lifespans sometimes measured in millions of years, a caldera that has not produced an eruption in tens of thousands of years may be considered dormant instead of extinct. An individual volcano in a monogenetic volcanic field can be extinct, but that does not mean a completely new volcano might not erupt close by with little or no warning, as its field may have an active magma supply.

### Volcanic-alert level

The three common popular classifications of volcanoes can be subjective and some volcanoes thought to have been extinct have erupted again. To help prevent people from falsely believing they are not at risk when living on or near a volcano, countries have adopted new classifications to describe the various levels and stages of volcanic activity. Some alert systems use different numbers or colours to designate the different stages. Other systems use colours and words. Some systems use a combination of both.

## Decade volcanoes

The Decade Volcanoes are 16 volcanoes identified by the [International Association of Volcanology and Chemistry of the Earth's Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Volcanology_and_Chemistry_of_the_Earth's_Interior) (IAVCEI) as being worthy of particular study in light of their history of large, destructive eruptions and proximity to populated areas. They are named Decade Volcanoes because the project was initiated as part of the United Nations-sponsored [International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Decade_for_Natural_Disaster_Reduction) (the 1990s). The 16 current Decade Volcanoes are:

- [Avachinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avachinsky)-[Koryaksky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koryaksky) (grouped together), [Kamchatka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamchatka), Russia
- [Nevado de Colima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevado_de_Colima), [Jalisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jalisco) and [Colima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colima), Mexico
- [Mount Etna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Etna), Sicily, Italy
- [Galeras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeras), [Nariño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nariño), Colombia
- [Mauna Loa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauna_Loa), Hawaii, US
- [Mount Merapi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Merapi), [Central Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Java), Indonesia
- [Mount Nyiragongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Nyiragongo), Democratic Republic of the Congo
- [Mount Rainier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier), [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_%28state%29), US
- [Sakurajima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakurajima), [Kagoshima Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kagoshima_Prefecture), Japan
- [Santa Maria/Santiaguito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_María_%28volcano%29), Guatemala
- [Santorini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorini), [Cyclades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclades), Greece
- [Taal Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taal_Volcano), [Luzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luzon), Philippines
- [Teide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teide), Canary Islands, Spain
- [Ulawun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulawun), [New Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Britain), Papua New Guinea
- [Mount Unzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Unzen), [Nagasaki Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagasaki_Prefecture), Japan
- [Vesuvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesuvius), [Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Naples), Italy

The [Deep Earth Carbon Degassing Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Earth_Carbon_Degassing_Project), an initiative of the [Deep Carbon Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Carbon_Observatory), monitors nine volcanoes, two of which are Decade volcanoes. The focus of the Deep Earth Carbon Degassing Project is to use [Multi-Component Gas Analyzer System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Component_Gas_Analyzer_System) instruments to measure CO2/SO2 ratios in real-time and in high-resolution to allow detection of the pre-eruptive degassing of rising magmas, improving [prediction of volcanic activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prediction_of_volcanic_activity).

## Volcanoes and humans

Volcanic eruptions pose a significant threat to human civilization. However, volcanic activity has also provided humans with important resources.

### Hazards

There are many different [types of volcanic eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Types_of_volcanic_eruptions) and associated activity: [phreatic eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phreatic_eruptions) (steam-generated eruptions), explosive eruptions of high-[silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica) lava (e.g., [rhyolite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyolite)), effusive eruptions of low-silica lava (e.g., [basalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt)), [sector collapses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sector_collapse), [pyroclastic flows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroclastic_flow), [lahars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahar) (debris flows) and [volcanic gas emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_gas). These can pose a hazard to humans. Earthquakes, [hot springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_spring), [fumaroles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumarole), [mud pots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud_pot) and [geysers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geyser) often accompany volcanic activity.

Volcanic gases can reach the stratosphere, where they form [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid) aerosols that can reflect solar radiation and lower surface temperatures significantly. Sulfur dioxide from the eruption of [Huaynaputina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaynaputina) may have caused the [Russian famine of 1601–1603](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_famine_of_1601–1603). Chemical reactions of sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere can also damage the [ozone layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone_layer), and acids such as [hydrogen chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_chloride) (HCl) and hydrogen fluoride (HF) can fall to the ground as [acid rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_rain). Excessive fluoride salts from eruptions have poisoned livestock in Iceland on multiple occasions. [Explosive volcanic eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosive_eruption) release the greenhouse gas [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide) and thus provide a deep source of [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon) for [biogeochemical cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biogeochemical_cycle).

Ash thrown into the air by eruptions can present a hazard to aircraft, especially [jet aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_aircraft) where the particles can be melted by the high operating temperature; the melted particles then adhere to the [turbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbine) blades and alter their shape, disrupting the operation of the turbine. This can cause major disruptions to air travel.

A [volcanic winter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_winter) is thought to have taken place around 70,000 years ago after the [supereruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supereruption) of [Lake Toba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Toba) on Sumatra island in Indonesia. This may have created a [population bottleneck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toba_catastrophe_theory) that affected the genetic inheritance of all humans today. Volcanic eruptions may have contributed to major extinction events, such as the [End-Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician-Silurian_extinction_events), [Permian-Triassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian-Triassic), and [Late Devonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Devonian_extinction) [mass extinctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_extinction).

The 1815 eruption of [Mount Tambora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Tambora) created global climate anomalies that became known as the "[Year Without a Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer)" because of the effect on North American and European weather. The freezing winter of 1740–41, which led to widespread [famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Famine_%281740–1741%29) in northern Europe, may also owe its origins to a volcanic eruption.

### Benefits

Although volcanic eruptions pose considerable hazards to humans, past volcanic activity has created important economic resources. Tuff formed from volcanic ash is a relatively soft rock, and it has been used for construction since ancient times. The Romans often used tuff, which is abundant in Italy, for construction. The [Rapa Nui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapa_Nui) people used tuff to make most of the *[moai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moai)* statues in [Easter Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Island).

Volcanic ash and weathered basalt produce some of the most fertile soil in the world, rich in nutrients such as iron, magnesium, potassium, calcium, and phosphorus. Volcanic activity is responsible for emplacing valuable mineral resources, such as metal ores. It is accompanied by high rates of heat flow from Earth's interior. These can be tapped as [geothermal power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geothermal_power).

Tourism associated with volcanoes is also a worldwide industry.

### Safety considerations

Many volcanoes near human settlements are heavily monitored with the aim of providing adequate advance warnings of imminent eruptions to nearby populations. Also, a better modern-day understanding of volcanology has led to some better informed governmental and public responses to unanticipated volcanic activities. While the science of volcanology may not yet be capable of predicting the exact times and dates of eruptions far into the future, on suitably monitored volcanoes the monitoring of ongoing volcanic indicators is often capable of predicting imminent eruptions with advance warnings minimally of hours, and usually of days prior to any eruptions. The diversity of volcanoes and their complexities mean that eruption forecasts for the foreseeable future will be based on [probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_theory), and the application of [risk management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk_management). Even then, some eruptions will have no useful warning. An example of this occurred in March 2017, when a tourist group was witnessing a presumed to be predictable Mount Etna eruption and the flowing lava came in contact with a snow accumulation causing a situational phreatic explosion causing injury to ten persons. Other types of significant eruptions are known to give useful warnings of only hours at the most by seismic monitoring. The recent demonstration of a magma chamber with repose times of tens of thousands of years, with potential for rapid recharge so potentially decreasing warning times, under the youngest volcano in central Europe, does not tell us if more careful monitoring will be useful.

Scientists are known to perceive risk, with its social elements, differently from local populations and those that undertake social risk assessments on their behalf, so that both disruptive false alarms and retrospective blame, when disasters occur, will continue to happen.

Thus in many cases, while volcanic eruptions may still cause major property destruction, the periodic large-scale loss of human life that was once associated with many volcanic eruptions, has recently been significantly reduced in areas where volcanoes are adequately monitored. This life-saving ability is derived via such volcanic-activity monitoring programs, through the greater abilities of local officials to facilitate timely evacuations based upon the greater modern-day knowledge of volcanism that is now available, and upon improved communications technologies such as cell phones. Such operations tend to provide enough time for humans to escape at least with their lives before a pending eruption. One example of such a recent successful volcanic evacuation was the [Mount Pinatubo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pinatubo) evacuation of 1991. This evacuation is believed to have saved 20,000 lives. In the case of [Mount Etna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Etna), a 2021 review found 77 deaths due to eruptions since 1536 but none since 1987.

Citizens who may be concerned about their own exposure to risk from nearby volcanic activity should familiarize themselves with the types of, and quality of, volcano monitoring and public notification procedures being employed by governmental authorities in their areas.

## Volcanoes on other celestial bodies

Earth's [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon) has no large volcanoes and no current volcanic activity, although recent evidence suggests it may still possess a partially molten core. However, the Moon does have many volcanic features such as [maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_mare) (the darker patches seen on the Moon), [rilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rille) and [domes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_dome).

The planet [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus) has a surface that is 90% [basalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt), indicating that volcanism played a major role in shaping its surface. The planet may have had a major global resurfacing event about 500 million years ago, from what scientists can tell from the density of impact craters on the surface. [Lava flows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava_flows) are widespread and forms of volcanism not present on Earth occur as well. Changes in the planet's atmosphere and observations of lightning have been attributed to ongoing volcanic eruptions, although there is no confirmation of whether or not Venus is still volcanically active. However, radar sounding by the Magellan probe revealed evidence for comparatively recent volcanic activity at Venus's highest volcano [Maat Mons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maat_Mons), in the form of [ash flows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ash_flow) near the summit and on the northern flank. However, the interpretation of the flows as ash flows has been questioned.

There are several extinct volcanoes on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars), four of which are vast shield volcanoes far bigger than any on Earth. They include [Arsia Mons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsia_Mons), [Ascraeus Mons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascraeus_Mons), [Hecates Tholus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecates_Tholus), [Olympus Mons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympus_Mons), and [Pavonis Mons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavonis_Mons). These volcanoes have been extinct for many millions of years, but the European *[Mars Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Express)* spacecraft has found evidence that volcanic activity may have occurred on Mars in the recent past as well.

[Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter)'s [moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_satellite) [Io](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Io_%28moon%29) is the most volcanically active object in the Solar System because of [tidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tides) interaction with Jupiter. It is covered with volcanoes that erupt [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur), [sulfur dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur_dioxide) and [silicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate) rock, and as a result, Io is constantly being resurfaced. Its lavas are the hottest known anywhere in the Solar System, with temperatures exceeding 1,800 K (1,500 °C). In February 2001, the largest recorded volcanic eruptions in the Solar System occurred on Io. [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_%28moon%29), the smallest of Jupiter's [Galilean moons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_moon), also appears to have an active volcanic system, except that its volcanic activity is entirely in the form of water, which freezes into ice on the frigid surface. This process is known as [cryovolcanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryovolcanism), and is apparently most common on the moons of the outer planets of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System).

In 1989, the *[Voyager 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_2)* spacecraft observed [cryovolcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryovolcano) (ice volcanoes) on [Triton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triton_%28moon%29), a [moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_satellite) of [Neptune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune), and in 2005 the *[Cassini–Huygens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassini–Huygens)* probe photographed [fountains of frozen particles erupting from Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_%28moon%29#Cryovolcanism), a moon of [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn). The ejecta may be composed of water, [liquid nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_nitrogen), [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia), dust, or [methane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane) compounds. *Cassini–Huygens* also found evidence of a methane-spewing cryovolcano on the [Saturnian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn) moon [Titan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_%28moon%29), which is believed to be a significant source of the methane found in its atmosphere. It is theorized that cryovolcanism may also be present on the [Kuiper Belt Object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuiper_Belt_Object) [Quaoar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaoar).

A 2010 study of the [exoplanet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoplanet) [COROT-7b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COROT-7b), which was detected by [transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit_method) in 2009, suggested that [tidal heating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_heating) from the host star very close to the planet and neighbouring planets could generate intense volcanic activity similar to that found on Io.

## History of volcano understanding

Volcanoes are not distributed evenly over the Earth's surface but active ones with significant impact were encountered early in human history, evidenced by footprints of [hominina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hominina) found in East African volcanic ash dated at 3.66 million years old. The association of volcanoes with fire and disaster is found in many oral traditions and had religious and thus social significance before the first written record of concepts related to volcanoes. Examples are: (1) the stories in the Athabascan subcultures about humans living inside mountains and a woman who uses fire to escape from a mountain, (2) [Pele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pele_%28deity%29)'s migration through the Hawarian island chain, ability to destroy forests and manifestations of the god's temper, and (3) the association in Javanese folklore of a king resident in [Mount Merapi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Merapi) volcano and a queen resident at a beach 50 km (31 mi) away on what is now known to be an earthquake fault that interacts with that volcano.

Many ancient accounts ascribe volcanic eruptions to [supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural) causes, such as the actions of [gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods) or [demigods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demigod). The earliest known such example is a neolithic goddess at [Çatalhöyük](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Çatalhöyük). The Ancient Greek god [Hephaistos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hephaistos) and the concepts of the underworld are aligned to volcanoes in that Greek culture.

However, others proposed more natural (but still incorrect) causes of volcanic activity. In the fifth century BC, [Anaxagoras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaxagoras) proposed eruptions were caused by a great wind. By 65 CE, [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger) proposed combustion as the cause, an idea also adopted by the [Jesuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit) [Athanasius Kircher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athanasius_Kircher) (1602–1680), who witnessed eruptions of [Mount Etna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Etna) and [Stromboli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stromboli), then visited the crater of [Vesuvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesuvius) and published his view of an Earth in *[Mundus Subterraneus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundus_Subterraneus)* with a central fire connected to numerous others depicting volcanoes as a type of safety valve. Edward Jorden, in his work on mineral waters, challenged this view; in 1632 he proposed [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur) "fermentation" as a heat source within Earth, Astronomer [Johannes Kepler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Kepler) (1571–1630) believed volcanoes were ducts for Earth's tears. In 1650, [René Descartes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/René_Descartes) proposed the core of Earth was incandescent and, by 1785, the works of Decartes and others were synthesized into geology by [James Hutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hutton) in his writings about [igneous intrusions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous_intrusion) of magma. [Lazzaro Spallanzani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazzaro_Spallanzani) had demonstrated by 1794 that steam explosions could cause explosive eruptions and many geologists held this as the universal cause of explosive eruptions up to the [1886 eruption of Mount Tarawera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1886_eruption_of_Mount_Tarawera) which allowed in one event differentiation of the concurrent [phreatomagmatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phreatomagmatic) and [hydrothermal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal) eruptions from dry explosive eruption, of, as it turned out, a basalt [dyke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dike_%28geology%29). [Alfred Lacroix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Lacroix) built upon his other knowledge with his studies on the [1902 eruption of Mount Pelée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1902_eruption_of_Mount_Pelée), and by 1928 [Arthur Holmes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Holmes) work had brought together the concepts of radioactive generation of heat, Earth's [mantle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantle_%28geology%29) structure, partial decompression melting of magma, and magma convection. This eventually led to the acceptance of plate tectonics.
